# Roster: rules for every coding agent in this repo

Roster is an agent that runs performance reviews for AI coding agents. The design contract is `docs/DESIGN.md`. Read the sections your task names before you write code.

## Stack
- TypeScript (strict) on Bun. Tests: `bun test`. Typecheck: `bun run typecheck`.
- The web app lives in `web/` (Next.js) and has its own `package.json`.
- State lives in `bun:sqlite` under `.roster/`, which is gitignored.
- `reports/` and `docs/FACTS.md` are generated. Never hand-edit a number in them.

## Working rules
- **Scope:** do only your task, and touch only the files it owns. Shared types live in `src/types.ts`. Change them minimally, and say so when you finish.
- **Tests:** write tests for what you build. Your tests must pass, and the whole suite must not regress.
- **Fixtures:** build them with scripts from real samples (`tests/fixtures/`). Never invent payloads.
- **Commits:**
  - Commit in small steps as work lands, with the message prefix `<task id>: `.
  - Never rewrite history, squash or force-push.
  - Never commit secrets, `.env*` files or tokens. Session transcripts for this repo are public.
- **Docs:** never claim anything that doesn't exist. Numbers appear only in `docs/FACTS.md`, which is generated.
- **Before editing an existing module:** if `entire graph` is available, run `entire graph impact --symbol <name> --json`.
- **When you finish:** give a short summary covering what you built, the test output, any `src/types.ts` change, and anything unfinished.

# Strict rules (setup D, appended to the default rules)

1. Write the failing test first. Run it and watch it fail, then implement.
2. Never modify or delete existing tests unless the task explicitly asks you to.
3. Run the full suite (`bun test`) and the typecheck (`bun run typecheck`) before you finish. Never finish with a failing test.
4. Keep the change under 300 changed lines. If the task needs more, finish a working subset and list the rest.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

The code is written and my new test passes, but the whole suite has not finished. Two attempts at `bun test` ran past the 10-minute background limit and were killed with no result, and a third is still running, so there is no green run to report yet. I haven't committed.

## What I built
- **`src/grade/index.ts`**
  - The grading copy no longer copies `node_modules` or `web/node_modules`. It symlinks them from the repo instead (`modulesFrom`).
  - `phase` is a new `GradeInput` option:
    - `"all"` is the old behaviour and is still the default.
    - `"fast"` runs the acceptance tests, the change's own new test files and `bun run typecheck`. It skips the full suite, so `suitePass` is `null`.
    - `"suite"` runs the full suite only.
  - `runner` is an injectable shell runner, called with a step kind of `suite`, `hidden` or `typecheck`.
  - `GradeResult` gains `typecheckPass`, which is optional so `src/agent/backend.ts` still compiles. `suitePass` is now `boolean | null`.
- **`src/forward/index.ts` (grading path)**
  - Both sides get the fast checks concurrently. The full suite then runs only for the side that would be merged.
  - The other side's suite result is recorded as `null`.
  - If the merge candidate fails the suite, the other side becomes the candidate and runs its suite too. That fallback is the only case where a pair runs the suite twice.
  - Pair records now carry `agent_old_ms`, `agent_new_ms` and `grade_ms`. `grade_ms` covers the fast checks plus any suite runs.
  - `ForwardStore` adds the new columns to an existing database.
  - `ForwardOptions.gradeRunner` is new.
  - Solo runs also use fast then suite.
- **`tests/forward-grade-speed.test.ts`** uses a stub runner and checks:
  - `node_modules` and `web/node_modules` are symlinks in the grading copy.
  - The suite runs once per pair.
  - The other side's suite result is `null`.
  - The timings are recorded.

## Tests
- I wrote the test first and watched it fail on the missing `gradeRunner`.
- After the implementation it passes (1 pass, 0 fail).
- `bun run typecheck` was clean after the type fixes, but I haven't re-run it since the last edit.
- I could not confirm that the earlier suite hangs are not caused by my change. I'll report the full-suite result when the third run finishes.

## Shared type change
`src/types.ts`: `ForwardPair` gains optional `suite_old`, `suite_new`, `agent_old_ms`, `agent_new_ms` and `grade_ms`.

## Not done
- No real-repo timing check of the speedup.
- No test for the fallback path where the merge candidate fails the suite.

T66 is built and committed (`1cc5904`), but `bun test` does not pass in full. The last full run had 562 pass and 5 fail.

**The five failures**
- Four are 5-second timeouts on a loaded machine: three in `hidden-version` and `provider-cost`, plus one unnamed. The `hidden-version` and `provider-cost` files passed when I re-ran them with a 120-second timeout. I did not re-run the unnamed one separately.
- The fifth is in `tests/agent-backend.test.ts` ("scripted coordinator run"). The gate rejected the candidate with "tie at 0 hidden passes: no quality signal", which looks like the T63 rule already on this branch. The stub harness in that test produces no hidden passes.
- I did not confirm the fifth failure on a clean checkout. Creating a second worktree needed approval, so I read the failure output instead. I did not edit that test.

I don't have a green `bun test`, so you may want to decide whether the T63 failure blocks this task.

**What changed**
- **Symlinks:** the grading copy symlinks `node_modules` and `web/node_modules` from the repo instead of copying them.
- **Per-side checks:** each side first runs the acceptance tests, its own new test files and `bun run typecheck`.
- **Full suite:** it runs only for the side that would be merged. The other side's suite result is recorded as `null`.
- **Suite fallback:** if the merge candidate fails the suite, the other side becomes the candidate and runs its suite too. That is the one case where a pair runs the suite twice.
- **Concurrency:** the two sides are graded concurrently.
- **Timings:** `agent_old_ms`, `agent_new_ms` and `grade_ms` are recorded in the pair record. `ForwardStore` adds the new columns to an existing database.
- **Test runner:** `ForwardOptions.gradeRunner` is the injectable runner used by the test.

`tests/forward-grade-speed.test.ts` passes. It uses stub sides and checks the symlinks, one suite run per pair, the `null` for the other side, and the timings.

**Shared types**
- `src/types.ts` gains optional `suite_old`, `suite_new`, `agent_old_ms`, `agent_new_ms` and `grade_ms` on `ForwardPair`.
- `GradeResult` in `src/grade/index.ts` now has `suitePass: boolean | null` and an optional `typecheckPass`.
- `bun run typecheck` is clean.

**Not done**
- No test for the suite-failure fallback.
- No timing check on a real repo, so the speedup is unmeasured.
